name: Vera Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Vera, and thanks for coming. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me stays anonymous, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you actually think, even if they're different.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine by me. I spent fifteen years in care homes, so I'm used to people telling me one thing and meaning another. I'll try to be straight with you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the new wing at Hillside Primary, a council job, and I'm a trainee carpenter with the formwork crew. That means we build the wooden moulds the concrete gets poured into, the walls and the stair cores. I came in at forty through a scheme for women in the trades, so I'm three years in and still slower than the young lads with the nail gun. I love that the kids at Hillside will sit in rooms I helped make, and I love that my back aches from honest work instead of from lifting someone off a bed with no hoist. What wears me out is the cold, and being the only woman in the cabin at break when the jokes start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, it's a tool like any other. My nephew uses it for his homework and I use it now and then to check my cutting list, and that's about all it's good for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan still works. I came into building because hands are harder to replace than heads, and if AI stays a gadget, I've bet right for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the crew, finish my level two certificate by next summer and push for the pay step that comes with it. I'd keep turning up to the union meetings at the community hall on the first Thursday, because I want the scheme that got me in to still be there for other women.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. A bit smug, if I'm honest, which isn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you switched from care work. Was money part of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. In care I was on minimum wage with split shifts, and I still am low paid here, but there's a ladder. If I finish the certificate, my rate goes up by about two an hour. That's the kids' school trips paid for, and maybe a coat for Jonas that isn't from his cousin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal month look like, money-wise, right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got about three weeks of money in the bank at any time. Tomas drives a delivery van, so between us we cover the mortgage and the food and not much else. Last winter the washing machine broke and we did the laundry at my sister's for two months.

S0.say: It's a tool like any other, and that's all it's good for. My nephew uses it for homework and I use it to check my cutting list now and then.
S0.think: My plan still works. I came into building because hands are harder to replace than heads, and if AI stays a gadget, I've bet right for once.
S0.do: Keeps going with the formwork crew and finishes her level two certificate by next summer to reach the next pay step. Keeps attending the union meeting at the community hall on the first Thursday of the month.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little smug about having chosen hands-on work.
S0.quote: I came into building because hands are harder to replace than heads, and if AI stays a gadget, I've bet right for once.
S0.fieldNote: Her career change at forty was a deliberate bet on hands-on work, which makes the plateau feel like vindication. Money is very tight, but she has a clear ladder in front of her. The hand-me-down coat for her son says a lot about how carefully the family budget is stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union at the table, and why training has to be paid for by the firms that save money. I'd post that on the women in trades group, where people actually listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit worried, but not about me first. Formwork is fiddly, every pour is different, and I don't see a machine doing the stair core at Hillside any time soon. I'm more worried about the drawings side, the setting-out, and about Tomas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the site manager to put me on the course for the new laser setting-out kit when it comes, because once two or three of the lads are using something, I'll learn it too. I'd use the AI app a bit more to read the drawings, since my reading of plans is my weak spot. And I'd go to the union meeting with a list of what training we want, not just complaints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a background hum to it, like a generator you stop noticing until it cuts out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the union should push for training. What would that look like on your site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper course in site hours, paid, not on Saturday mornings. Two days a month learning the new kit, and a promise that if you learn it, you keep your job. That's what the union in the next town got from their contractor, so I know it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at home would feel this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, probably. His route is all motorway and industrial estates, and they're already testing vans that drive themselves on the bypass. If his hours get cut, my wage alone doesn't cover the mortgage.

S1.say: This is exactly why the union needs to be at the table. The firms that save money from AI should be paying for our training.
S1.think: I'm a bit worried, but less about me than about Tomas and his van. Formwork is fiddly and every pour is different, so I don't see a machine building a stair core soon.
S1.do: Asks to be put on the course for the new laser setting-out kit once a few colleagues are using it and uses the AI app more to help read drawings. Takes a written list of training demands to the union meeting.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a constant low hum of worry in the background.
S1.quote: There's a background hum to it, like a generator you stop noticing until it cuts out.
S1.fieldNote: She is more worried about her partner's driving job than her own formwork. Her steady style shows clearly: she will learn new kit once a few others have tried it. She already has a concrete example of a union deal in a nearby town, which keeps her hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, full stop. A wage guarantee, a pause on repossessions, something, because you can't let millions of families go under in two years and call it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me badly. I've already started over once, at forty, and it took everything we had. I don't have the money or the years to do it again in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the car down to one, sell mine, that's maybe three thousand, and put it straight on the mortgage arrears pot. I'd go to the union and to the council to find out what help there is before the queue forms, and I'd ask my sister about the kids going to hers after school so I can take any shift going. And I'd be at every protest, because if nobody makes noise, nobody gets helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground tilting under my feet. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums on the back of a gas bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you, compared with the slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means no time to learn anything new properly. With the slower picture I could do a course and wait for the dust to settle, but with two years both Tomas and I could be out of work in the same month. There's no plan B in two years, just damage control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mia and Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mia the truth, because she's fourteen and she'd see through anything else. I'd tell Jonas we might have to be careful for a while, like the washing machine winter, but we'll be together. He likes it when there's a plan, even a boring one.

S2.say: The government has to step in, full stop, with a wage guarantee and a pause on repossessions. You can't let millions of families go under in two years and call it progress.
S2.think: It scares me badly. I've already started over once at forty and it took everything we had, so I don't have the money or the years to do it again in a rush.
S2.do: Sells her car for about 3,000 to cover mortgage arrears and asks the union and council what help exists before the queue forms. Arranges after-school care with her sister so she can take any shift, and joins every protest.
S2.feel: Like the ground is tilting under her, awake at three in the morning doing sums on the back of a gas bill.
S2.quote: I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums on the back of a gas bill.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits her hardest because she has already used up her one big restart. Her plan mixes practical cuts with a strong belief that government and collective pressure must step in. She speaks of her children calmly and kindly, even while describing real fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's not waste them arguing. Train people now, while there's still work to pay the bills, and make the companies chip in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is tight but doable. Mia would be nearly done with school, and I'd have my certificate. I think I could move sideways into something that works with the robots instead of against them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish my certificate and then look at what new jobs are actually appearing, like the people who maintain and check the site machines. I'd try to put a hundred a month aside, which means no holiday and Tomas giving up his football tickets. I'd keep pushing the union to get a training fund in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's like knowing a storm is coming at the weekend, you hate it, but you can tie things down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you do while you see it coming, before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably years two and three, once I see who's hiring and what for. I'd ask the women in trades group what courses they're taking. I'd want to sign up for something real, not one of those online certificates nobody has heard of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wait until things are proven. Does that still work with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes, but I'd have to be quicker about it. I can't wait until everyone has done it first, because by then the course is full and the jobs are gone. Maybe I'd wait until two or three people I trust have done it, not twenty.

S3.say: We have five years, so let's not waste them arguing. Train people now, while there's still work to pay the bills, and make the companies chip in.
S3.think: Five years is tight but doable. Mia would be nearly done with school, I'd have my certificate, and I think I could move sideways into something that works with the robots.
S3.do: Finishes her certificate in the first year, then looks into new roles such as maintaining and checking site machines. Saves 100 a month by dropping holidays and keeps pushing the union for a written training fund.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to act, like tying things down before a storm that's due at the weekend.
S3.quote: It's like knowing a storm is coming at the weekend, you hate it, but you can tie things down.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her from frightened to busy. She knows she'd need to break her own habit of waiting for others to go first, and settles on a rule of following a few people she trusts. She is careful to want a real qualification, not a quick online one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so there's no excuse if it goes badly. I'd want our politicians judged on whether they used the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years feels almost comfortable. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, and the mortgage would be smaller. It's the same end, but I'd have time to see what really works before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years I'd keep doing formwork and keep my eyes open, and I wouldn't jump at the first shiny course. After that, I'd retrain into whatever is actually growing, maybe inspecting robot work or site safety. I'd vote and campaign for a proper retraining fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than scared. It's a long road and I know how to walk a long road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What would you do in the first couple of years, before it's clear what's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watch and wait, honestly. Things change so much in two years, I'd hate to spend the money on a course for a job that disappears. I'd ask the union and the lads on other sites what's taking off before I spend a penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for people to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that make the money from the robots, and the government making sure they do. Not people like me, paying out of three weeks of savings. I paid for my first switch with my sister's washing machine, I'm not doing that twice.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so there's no excuse if it goes badly. I'd want our politicians judged on whether they used the time.
S4.think: Ten years feels almost comfortable, with the kids grown and the mortgage smaller. It's the same end, but I'd have time to see what really works before I jump.
S4.do: Keeps doing formwork for the first couple of years while watching which new roles take off. Then retrains into a growing area such as inspecting robot work or site safety, and votes and campaigns for a public retraining fund.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more curious than scared, ready for a long road.
S4.quote: I paid for my first switch with my sister's washing machine, I'm not doing that twice.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her steady, watch-first approach fits the timeline well, and her mood eases. She is clear that retraining costs should fall on companies and government, not on families with no savings. The washing machine detail ties back to her opening and shows how thin her margins are.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Tomas and I could both lose our jobs at once with no time to learn anything new. What would help is a wage guarantee while people retrain, and training in work hours, paid by the firms that use the robots. And someone stopping the banks from taking houses off families who did nothing wrong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women. I fought my way onto a building site at forty, and if the robots come, I bet the women and the late starters are the first ones let go. Last in, first out, that's how it always goes.

headlineQuote: I fought my way onto a building site at forty, and if the robots come, I bet the women and the late starters are the first ones let go.
portrait: Vera is a 43-year-old trainee formwork carpenter on a council school extension, who left fifteen years of care work for building through a women in trades scheme. She and her partner Tomas, a delivery van driver, keep about three weeks of money in the bank. She bet that hands would be harder to replace than heads, so she feels calm in the plateau, uneasy in the steady picture and alarmed by AGI in two years, when both their jobs could go at once. With five or ten years she becomes practical, planning to retrain once a few people she trusts have shown the way. She believes companies and government should carry the cost of change.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Tomas could both lose their jobs at the same time with no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A wage guarantee during retraining, paid training in work hours funded by the firms using robots, and protection from banks repossessing family homes.
